title: NGC 6791: Full Hubble ACS Field
caption: Open star cluster NGC 6791, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6791 · constellation Lyra · about 13,300 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Stars crowd the full field of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, and two background galaxies show through at upper left. This is NGC 6791, an ancient open star cluster 13,300 light-years away in Lyra, whose ordinary stars are estimated to be 8 billion years old. NGC 6791 ranks among the oldest and largest known open clusters, about 10 times larger than most, with roughly 10,000 stars.

Hubble studied the dimmest stars in the cluster, white dwarfs, the burned-out remains of Sun-like stars. Because they cool at a predictable rate, they work as clocks. In NGC 6791 they gave odd readings. One group looked 6 billion years old and another 4 billion, though stars in an open cluster should share one age.

The team found that the younger-looking group may be made of binary pairs, which at this distance blur into single, brighter points that look younger. That leaves two ages to reconcile, 8 billion years for the normal stars and 6 billion for the white dwarfs, which would need some process slowing white-dwarf evolution.

understand.summary: A composite of exposures from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys in visible and near-infrared light. F606W is shown in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The exposures total about 6 hours, revealing white dwarfs far too faint for the eye, and the F814W filter records near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

behind.people: See full credit: NASA, ESA, and L. Bedin (STScI)
behind.exposure: Observation dates per NASA: July 2003, July 2005, Exposure Time: 6 hours.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Most star clusters are too far away, and their white dwarfs too faint, for ground-based telescopes to see. Binary stars are common among ordinary stars in NGC 6791 and in many other clusters, but finding them among white dwarfs would be a first.
sources: NASA release: What’s My Age? Mystery Star Cluster Has 3 Different Birthdays
